title: 59 Identification of parasitic dairy goats using Bio-Electrical Impedance Analysis
content:
Abstract
Parasitic infections, particularly those caused by Haemonchus contortus, pose significant challenges to the dairy goat industry, leading to anemia, reduced productivity, compromised health and increased mortality. Effective detection and management of parasitic burdens are critical for maintaining herd health and optimizing production. This study aimed to differentiate parasitized dairy goats from healthy ones using a Bio-Electrical Impedance device combined with hematological and parasitological indicators. A total of 12 goats were used for this study, which were randomly divided into two groups: six healthy goats dewormed two weeks prior to the study and six naturally parasitized animals. All goats were allowed to graze on natural vegetation for four months (July-October) in separate paddocks with access to ad libitum hay and water and a grain supplement. Parameters assessed weekly for each goat included electrical resistance (R), reactance (Xc), FAMACHA score, fecal egg count (FEC), and blood packed cell volume (PCV). The FEC and PCV values differed significantly between the groups. Healthy goats exhibited FEC of 987 ± 46 eggs per gram, compared to 2208 ± 50 eggs per gram in parasitized goats (P < 0.001). The PCV values were higher in healthy goats (25.6 ± 0.2%) than in parasitized ones (24.7 ± 0.2% P < 0.001), indicating anemia due to blood-feeding parasites. Electric Resistance (R) was slightly higher in parasitized goats (480.5 ± 20.0 Ω) compared to healthy goats (498.9 ± 18.4 Ω), suggesting potential dehydration and tissue changes, though differences were not statistically significant. Reactance (Xc) was marginally reduced in parasitized goats (505.9 ± 30.4 Ω) compared to healthy goats (487.1 ± 28.0 Ω). FAMACHA scores and their correlation with PCV and FEC further validated the physiological impacts of parasitic loads, with parasitized goats scoring higher, indicative of anemia severity. The integration of FEC and PCV with BIA metrics highlighted their combined utility for accurately distinguishing between healthy and parasitized goats. The study’s findings emphasize the potential of integrating BIA with traditional diagnostic tools to enhance the precision of parasitic detection. BIA, being non-invasive and rapid, provides a promising alternative to labor-intensive fecal egg counting, and while PCV and FAMACHA scoring offer critical hematological and parasitological data, this approach offers enhanced diagnostic precision and facilitates timely intervention. This study demonstrates the potential of BIA in a parasite management program, and its integration with traditional measures (FEC and PCV) enhances the accuracy of parasitic infection detection. This integrative approach has the potential to enhance decision-making, improve animal welfare, and reduce economic losses in the dairy goat industry.
